blocks.en: The Gospel of the King
blocks.es_reference: El Evangelio del Rey

blocks.en: Matthew sat down to write the first book of the New Testament with one great aim: to prove to his own people that Jesus of Nazareth is the King they had waited for — the Messiah promised in the Law and the Prophets. From first verse to last he keeps sounding one note: this was done that it might be fulfilled. He is the Gospel of fulfillment. Again and again he reaches back into the Old Testament and shows that the story which began with Abraham and ran through David has come to its appointed end in a child born in Bethlehem. So before we ever reach the Sermon on the Mount or a single parable, Matthew spends two chapters telling us who this child is and where He came from. He answers the question of identity first, because everything else in the book depends on the answer.
blocks.es_reference: Mateo se sentó a escribir el primer libro del Nuevo Testamento con un gran propósito: probar a su propio pueblo que Jesús de Nazaret es el Rey que habían esperado — el Mesías prometido en la Ley y los Profetas. Del primer versículo al último repite una sola nota: esto fue hecho para que se cumpliese. Es el Evangelio del cumplimiento. Una y otra vez se remonta al Antiguo Testamento y muestra que la historia que comenzó con Abraham y corrió por medio de David ha llegado a su fin señalado en un niño nacido en Belén. Así que antes de llegar al Sermón del Monte o a una sola parábola, Mateo dedica dos capítulos a decirnos quién es este niño y de dónde vino. Responde primero la pregunta de la identidad, porque todo lo demás en el libro depende de la respuesta.

blocks.en: A Gospel That Begins with a Genealogy
blocks.es_reference: Un Evangelio Que Comienza con una Genealogía

blocks.en: It strikes the modern reader as a strange way to open a book — forty-some names, most of them hard to pronounce, "Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob," and on it goes. We are tempted to skip it and get to the story. But Matthew is not wasting our time; he is laying a foundation. The very first line tells us what the list is for: "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the Son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Two names tower over the rest. Son of David means Jesus is the rightful King, the heir of David's throne, the One of whom the prophets said His kingdom would have no end. Son of Abraham means He is the One in whom, as God promised Abraham, all the families of the earth would be blessed — not the Jews only, but the nations. The genealogy is Matthew's way of saying: this is no accident of history. God has been working toward this child for two thousand years.
blocks.es_reference: Al lector moderno le parece una manera extraña de abrir un libro — unos cuarenta nombres, la mayoría difíciles de pronunciar, "Abraham engendró a Isaac, Isaac engendró a Jacob," y así sigue. Sentimos la tentación de saltarlo y llegar a la historia. Pero Mateo no nos hace perder el tiempo; está poniendo un fundamento. La primera línea nos dice para qué es la lista: "Libro de la genealogía de Jesucristo, hijo de David, hijo de Abraham" (Mateo 1:1). Dos nombres se elevan sobre los demás. Hijo de David significa que Jesús es el Rey legítimo, el heredero del trono de David, Aquel de quien los profetas dijeron que su reino no tendría fin. Hijo de Abraham significa que Él es Aquel en quien, como Dios prometió a Abraham, todas las familias de la tierra serían bendecidas — no los judíos solamente, sino las naciones. La genealogía es la manera de Mateo de decir: esto no es un accidente de la historia. Dios ha estado obrando hacia este niño por dos mil años.

blocks.en: Matthew arranges the list in three sets of fourteen — from Abraham to David, from David to the exile, from the exile to Christ. He is showing a deliberate pattern, a history moving on purpose toward a goal. The reader is meant to feel the long ache of waiting, and then the relief of arrival.
blocks.es_reference: Mateo ordena la lista en tres grupos de catorce — de Abraham a David, de David al destierro, del destierro a Cristo. Muestra un patrón deliberado, una historia que avanza con propósito hacia una meta. El lector ha de sentir la larga espera, y luego el alivio de la llegada.

blocks.en: Grace in the Family Tree
blocks.es_reference: Gracia en el Árbol Genealógico

blocks.en: Then comes a surprise a careful reader of the ancient world would never expect. Jewish genealogies traced the fathers; women were rarely named. Yet Matthew names four — and not the great matriarchs Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel, but four whose stories carry the mark of the outsider or the memory of scandal. There is Tamar, who deceived Judah; Rahab, the harlot of Jericho, a Gentile; Ruth, the virtuous Moabite whose own people had a fraught history with Israel (Deuteronomy 23:3), yet who is praised in her own book as a woman of noble character; and the wife of Uriah, Bathsheba, named in a way that recalls David's great sin. Why hang these names on the family tree of the King? Because the gospel is already in the genealogy. Grace runs in this bloodline. The Savior who came to save His people from their sins was not ashamed to be born into a line of sinners and strangers. If you have ever felt your past disqualifies you, look at the list. There is room in His family for the outsider and the failure. There is room for you.
blocks.es_reference: Entonces viene una sorpresa que un lector cuidadoso del mundo antiguo jamás esperaría. Las genealogías judías trazaban a los padres; rara vez se nombraba a las mujeres. Sin embargo, Mateo nombra a cuatro — y no a las grandes matriarcas Sara, Rebeca y Raquel, sino a cuatro cuyas historias llevan la marca del extranjero o el recuerdo del escándalo. Está Tamar, que engañó a Judá; Rahab, la ramera de Jericó, una gentil; Rut, la virtuosa moabita cuyo propio pueblo tuvo una historia tensa con Israel (Deuteronomio 23:3), pero que es alabada en su propio libro como una mujer de carácter noble; y la mujer de Urías, Betsabé, nombrada de un modo que recuerda el gran pecado de David. ¿Por qué colgar estos nombres en el árbol genealógico del Rey? Porque el evangelio ya está en la genealogía. La gracia corre por esta sangre. El Salvador que vino a salvar a su pueblo de sus pecados no se avergonzó de nacer en una línea de pecadores y extranjeros. Si alguna vez ha sentido que su pasado lo descalifica, mire la lista. Hay lugar en su familia para el de afuera y para el que falló. Hay lugar para usted.

blocks.en: You Shall Call His Name Jesus
blocks.es_reference: Llamarás Su Nombre Jesús

blocks.en: When Joseph learns Mary is with child, he is a righteous man caught in an agonizing choice, and he resolves to put her away quietly rather than expose her. But an angel comes to him in a dream: "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take to you Mary your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. And she will bring forth a Son, and you shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:20-21). The name Jesus means "the LORD saves." It tells us in a single word why He came — not merely to be admired, not merely to teach, but to save, and to save not from Rome or from poverty but from the deepest bondage of all, the bondage of sin. And mark Joseph: told to do a hard thing, he simply obeys. We will see him obey again and again in these two chapters, asking no questions, moving when God says move. He is the quiet model of the faith Matthew commends.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando José se entera de que María está encinta, es un hombre justo atrapado en una decisión angustiosa, y resuelve dejarla en secreto en vez de exponerla. Pero un ángel viene a él en sueños: "José, hijo de David, no temas recibir a María tu esposa, porque lo que en ella es engendrado, del Espíritu Santo es. Y dará a luz un hijo, y llamarás su nombre JESÚS, porque él salvará a su pueblo de sus pecados" (Mateo 1:20-21). El nombre Jesús significa "el SEÑOR salva." Nos dice en una sola palabra por qué vino — no meramente a ser admirado, no meramente a enseñar, sino a salvar, y a salvar no de Roma ni de la pobreza sino de la más profunda esclavitud de todas, la esclavitud del pecado. Y note a José: mandado a hacer algo difícil, sencillamente obedece. Lo veremos obedecer una y otra vez en estos dos capítulos, sin preguntar, moviéndose cuando Dios dice muévete. Es el modelo callado de la fe que Mateo elogia.

blocks.en: Immanuel — God With Us
blocks.es_reference: Emanuel — Dios con Nosotros

blocks.en: Matthew then lifts our eyes from the name Jesus to the name Immanuel, citing the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and bear a Son, and they shall call His name Immanuel," which means "God with us" (Matthew 1:23, quoting Isaiah 7:14). Here is Matthew's boldest claim. This child is not only the King in David's line; He is God come down to dwell with us. There are those who will grant that Jesus was a good man, a great teacher, even a prophet, and stop there, denying His deity. But this single name will not let us stop there. Immanuel. God with us. The whole of the Christian faith stands or falls on it: in this child the Maker of the heavens has entered His own creation. What an assurance it is to know that God is not far off and watching, but near — with us. He is with us; He is for us; and by His Spirit He comes to be in us.
blocks.es_reference: Mateo entonces levanta nuestros ojos del nombre Jesús al nombre Emanuel, citando al profeta Isaías: "He aquí, una virgen concebirá y dará a luz un hijo, y llamarás su nombre Emanuel," que significa "Dios con nosotros" (Mateo 1:23, citando Isaías 7:14). Aquí está la afirmación más audaz de Mateo. Este niño no es solo el Rey en la línea de David; es Dios que ha descendido a morar con nosotros. Hay quienes conceden que Jesús fue un buen hombre, un gran maestro, hasta un profeta, y se detienen allí, negando su deidad. Pero este solo nombre no nos deja detenernos allí. Emanuel. Dios con nosotros. Toda la fe cristiana se sostiene o cae en ello: en este niño el Hacedor de los cielos ha entrado en su propia creación. ¡Qué seguridad es saber que Dios no está lejos observando, sino cerca — con nosotros! Él está con nosotros; Él es por nosotros; y por su Espíritu viene a estar en nosotros.

blocks.en: A Note on Fulfillment: Double-Fulfillment and Typology
blocks.es_reference: Una Nota sobre el Cumplimiento: Doble Cumplimiento y Tipología

blocks.en: Matthew's word "fulfilled" raises a question thoughtful students rightly ask. When Isaiah spoke of Immanuel, he was speaking to a real king in a real crisis seven hundred years before Bethlehem. How then is it "fulfilled" in Jesus? Here we meet what is, among evangelicals, a common interpretation: many of these prophecies have a double fulfillment. What God did once in history through the nation of Israel or through an individual, He brought to its true and final completion in Jesus. The Old Testament event is real in its own day, and it is also a pattern — a type — that points beyond itself to Christ. This typological reading has long been defended by careful scholars such as Albert Barnes and Walter Kaiser.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra "cumplido" de Mateo plantea una pregunta que los estudiantes reflexivos hacen con razón. Cuando Isaías habló de Emanuel, hablaba a un rey real en una crisis real setecientos años antes de Belén. ¿Cómo, entonces, se "cumple" en Jesús? Aquí encontramos lo que es, entre los evangélicos, una interpretación común: muchas de estas profecías tienen un doble cumplimiento. Lo que Dios hizo una vez en la historia por medio de la nación de Israel o de un individuo, lo llevó a su verdadera y final consumación en Jesús. El evento del Antiguo Testamento es real en su propio día, y es también un patrón — un tipo — que apunta más allá de sí mismo a Cristo. Esta lectura tipológica ha sido defendida por mucho tiempo por eruditos cuidadosos como Albert Barnes y Walter Kaiser.

blocks.en: Take Isaiah 7:14 itself. The sign of Immanuel was given to King Ahaz, who, threatened by an alliance of enemies, was tempted to trust a scheming alliance with Assyria rather than the LORD. Isaiah told him to ask God for a sign; Ahaz hypocritically refused, and Isaiah declared God would give a sign anyway — a child called Immanuel. It would have meant little to Ahaz if the sign lay seven hundred years in his future; there was a fulfillment in his own day, likely in the birth of a child whose growing-up marked God's deliverance. And yet the words reach past Ahaz to a greater Son, conceived not by man but by the Holy Spirit, who alone could be the true and full Immanuel, God with us.
blocks.es_reference: Tómese Isaías 7:14 mismo. La señal de Emanuel fue dada al rey Acaz, quien, amenazado por una alianza de enemigos, fue tentado a confiar en una alianza tramposa con Asiria en vez de en el SEÑOR. Isaías le dijo que pidiera a Dios una señal; Acaz hipócritamente se negó, e Isaías declaró que Dios daría una señal de todos modos — un niño llamado Emanuel. Poco habría significado para Acaz si la señal estuviera setecientos años en su futuro; hubo un cumplimiento en su propio día, probablemente en el nacimiento de un niño cuyo crecer marcó la liberación de Dios. Y sin embargo las palabras alcanzan más allá de Acaz a un Hijo mayor, concebido no por varón sino por el Espíritu Santo, quien solo podía ser el verdadero y pleno Emanuel, Dios con nosotros.

blocks.en: The same pattern runs through Scripture. Hosea 11:1 — "Out of Egypt I called My son" — looks back to the nation of Israel coming out of Egypt in the Exodus; Matthew sees it fulfilled again when the child Jesus is brought up out of Egypt. Isaiah 53, the suffering servant, speaks of a people who suffer and are restored, and finds its deepest fulfillment in the rejection and atoning death of Christ. Psalm 22 sings of David's own anguish — the pierced hands, the mockery, the divided garments — and is taken up almost word for word at the cross. And the forty years Israel wandered in the wilderness reappear in the forty days of Jesus' temptation, where He, the true Israel, succeeds in resisting the tempter exactly where the nation failed. This is what scholars call recapitulation: Jesus relives Israel's story and gets it right. God often works things in parallel. The first event is true; the second is truer still.
blocks.es_reference: El mismo patrón corre por la Escritura. Oseas 11:1 — "De Egipto llamé a mi hijo" — mira atrás a la nación de Israel saliendo de Egipto en el Éxodo; Mateo lo ve cumplirse de nuevo cuando el niño Jesús es sacado de Egipto. Isaías 53, el siervo sufriente, habla de un pueblo que sufre y es restaurado, y halla su cumplimiento más profundo en el rechazo y la muerte expiatoria de Cristo. El Salmo 22 canta la propia angustia de David — las manos horadadas, la burla, los vestidos repartidos — y es tomado casi palabra por palabra en la cruz. Y los cuarenta años que Israel vagó en el desierto reaparecen en los cuarenta días de la tentación de Jesús, donde Él, el verdadero Israel, logra resistir al tentador exactamente donde la nación falló. Esto es lo que los eruditos llaman recapitulación: Jesús revive la historia de Israel y la hace bien. Dios a menudo obra las cosas en paralelo. El primer evento es verdadero; el segundo es aún más verdadero.

blocks.en: Wise Men and a Frightened King
blocks.es_reference: Magos y un Rey Atemorizado

blocks.en: In the second chapter the scene shifts. Wise men — Magi — come from the East following a star, asking, "Where is He who has been born King of the Jews? For we have seen His star... and have come to worship Him" (Matthew 2:2). Here is a wonder Matthew wants us to feel: the first worshipers to seek out the newborn King are Gentiles, foreigners from a distant land, while Jerusalem, the city of God, sleeps. The Son of Abraham has come, and already the nations are being drawn in. The Magi bring gifts that preach their own small sermon: gold, the tribute fit for a king; frankincense, the incense of worship offered to God; and myrrh, a spice used to anoint the dead — a shadow, even at the cradle, of the cross to come.
blocks.es_reference: En el segundo capítulo la escena cambia. Unos magos vienen del oriente siguiendo una estrella, preguntando: "¿Dónde está el rey de los judíos, que ha nacido? Porque su estrella hemos visto... y venimos a adorarle" (Mateo 2:2). He aquí una maravilla que Mateo quiere que sintamos: los primeros adoradores en buscar al Rey recién nacido son gentiles, extranjeros de una tierra lejana, mientras Jerusalén, la ciudad de Dios, duerme. El Hijo de Abraham ha venido, y ya las naciones están siendo atraídas. Los magos traen regalos que predican su propio pequeño sermón: oro, el tributo digno de un rey; incienso, la adoración ofrecida a Dios; y mirra, una especia usada para ungir a los muertos — una sombra, aun en la cuna, de la cruz por venir.

blocks.en: But there is another king in the story. When Herod hears of a newborn King of the Jews he does not rejoice; he is troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. Matthew sets two kings side by side, and the contrast could not be sharper. One is a King who comes to save His people; the other is a king who, to guard his own throne, will murder a village of children. Herod, outwitted in his plot to use the Magi as informants, flies into a rage and orders the slaughter of the baby boys of Bethlehem. Matthew hears in it the cry of the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted, because they are no more" (Matthew 2:18). From the very beginning, the coming of the King is met by the violence of a world that loves its own power.
blocks.es_reference: Pero hay otro rey en la historia. Cuando Herodes oye de un Rey de los judíos recién nacido, no se regocija; se turba, y toda Jerusalén con él. Mateo pone dos reyes lado a lado, y el contraste no podría ser más agudo. Uno es un Rey que viene a salvar a su pueblo; el otro es un rey que, para guardar su propio trono, asesinará a una aldea de niños. Herodes, burlado en su plan de usar a los magos como informantes, monta en cólera y ordena la matanza de los niños varones de Belén. Mateo oye en ello el clamor del profeta Jeremías: "Voz fue oída en Ramá, lamentación, lloro y gemido grande; Raquel que llora a sus hijos, y no quiso ser consolada, porque perecieron" (Mateo 2:18). Desde el mismísimo comienzo, la venida del Rey es recibida por la violencia de un mundo que ama su propio poder.

blocks.en: Out of Egypt
blocks.es_reference: De Egipto

blocks.en: Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the child and His mother by night and flees to Egypt, and there they remain until Herod is dead. Matthew tells us this happened "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son'" (Matthew 2:15). Israel of old went down into Egypt and was brought up out of it; now the true Son of God retraces that path. When at last they return, they settle in Nazareth, and even that lowly, despised town fulfills what the prophets foreshadowed: "He shall be called a Nazarene" (Matthew 2:23).
blocks.es_reference: Avisado en sueños, José toma al niño y a su madre de noche y huye a Egipto, y allí permanecen hasta la muerte de Herodes. Mateo nos dice que esto sucedió "para que se cumpliese lo que dijo el Señor por medio del profeta, diciendo: De Egipto llamé a mi Hijo" (Mateo 2:15). El Israel de antaño descendió a Egipto y fue sacado de allí; ahora el verdadero Hijo de Dios vuelve a recorrer ese camino. Cuando al fin regresan, se establecen en Nazaret, y aun ese pueblo humilde y despreciado cumple lo que los profetas habían anunciado: "Será llamado nazareno" (Mateo 2:23).

blocks.en: The Whole Gospel in Two Chapters
blocks.es_reference: Todo el Evangelio en Dos Capítulos

blocks.en: Before a word of His preaching, before a single miracle, Matthew has told us all we most need to know. This child is the Son of David, the rightful King. He is the Son of Abraham, in whom the nations will be blessed. He is Jesus, who will save His people from their sins. He is Immanuel, God with us. He is the true Israel, fulfilling in Himself the whole long story of His people. And already the world is divided over Him — Gentiles on their knees, a king with a sword, a mother weeping, a father quietly obeying. The King has come. The only question Unit 1 leaves with you is the question the Magi answered with their gifts and Herod answered with his sword: what will you do with Him?
blocks.es_reference: Antes de una palabra de su predicación, antes de un solo milagro, Mateo nos ha dicho todo lo que más necesitamos saber. Este niño es el Hijo de David, el Rey legítimo. Es el Hijo de Abraham, en quien las naciones serán bendecidas. Es Jesús, quien salvará a su pueblo de sus pecados. Es Emanuel, Dios con nosotros. Es el verdadero Israel, cumpliendo en sí mismo toda la larga historia de su pueblo. Y ya el mundo está dividido por causa de Él — gentiles de rodillas, un rey con espada, una madre que llora, un padre que calladamente obedece. El Rey ha venido. La única pregunta que la Unidad 1 le deja es la pregunta que los magos respondieron con sus regalos y Herodes respondió con su espada: ¿qué hará usted con Él?

blocks.en: "And you shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins." — Matthew 1:21 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Y dará a luz un hijo, y llamarás su nombre JESÚS; porque él salvará a su pueblo de sus pecados." — Mateo 1:21 (RVG)

mc.why: Matthew begins with the genealogy to lay a foundation for who Jesus is.

mc.stem: By calling Jesus 'the Son of David,' Matthew identifies Him as:
options: The promised King and heir of David's throne
mc.why: 'Son of David' marks Jesus as the rightful King in David's line.

mc.stem: The genealogy surprisingly names several women (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba). Their inclusion highlights:
options: God's grace reaching sinners and outsiders
mc.why: The four women show grace running through the bloodline of the King.

mc.stem: According to Matthew 1:21, Joseph is to name the child 'Jesus' because:
options: He will save His people from their sins
He will be a great teacher
mc.why: The name Jesus means 'the LORD saves'; He came to save from sin.

mc.stem: The name 'Immanuel' means:
mc.why: Immanuel means 'God with us' — a claim to Christ's deity.

mc.stem: Matthew 1:23 quotes which prophet for the sign of the virgin birth?
mc.why: Matthew cites Isaiah 7:14 for the sign of Immanuel.

mc.stem: In its original setting, the sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14) was given to which king?
mc.why: The sign was first given to King Ahaz in his own crisis.

mc.stem: The 'double-fulfillment' view of prophecy holds that:
options: A prophecy can have a near fulfillment and a greater, final fulfillment in Christ
mc.why: A prophecy may be fulfilled in its own day and again, more fully, in Christ.

mc.stem: Hosea 11:1, 'Out of Egypt I called My son,' originally referred to:
options: The nation of Israel's exodus from Egypt
mc.why: Hosea looks back to Israel coming up out of Egypt in the Exodus.

mc.stem: Matthew 2:15 applies 'Out of Egypt I called My Son' to:
options: Jesus being brought up out of Egypt
mc.why: Matthew sees the prophecy fulfilled again in the child Jesus.

mc.stem: The idea that Jesus relives Israel's story and succeeds where the nation failed (40 years / 40 days) is called:
mc.why: Recapitulation: Jesus, the true Israel, relives the story and gets it right.

mc.stem: The wise men (Magi) who sought the newborn King came from:
mc.why: The Magi came from the East, following the star.

mc.stem: That Gentile Magi were the first to seek and worship the newborn King shows that:
options: The Jews rejected Him from birth
Jesus is King for all nations, not the Jews only
mc.why: The Son of Abraham draws the nations in; the gospel reaches the Gentiles.

mc.stem: When Herod heard of a newborn King of the Jews, he responded with:
mc.why: Herod was troubled and plotted to destroy the child.

mc.stem: The gifts the Magi brought were:
mc.why: Gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh foreshadowing His death.

mc.stem: To destroy the newborn King, Herod ordered:
options: The killing of the male children of Bethlehem
mc.why: Herod ordered the slaughter of the baby boys of Bethlehem.

mc.stem: Matthew quotes Jeremiah's words, 'Rachel weeping for her children,' in connection with:
options: The birth of John the Baptist
Herod's massacre of the children of Bethlehem
mc.why: The prophet's lament is heard in the weeping over Bethlehem's children.

mc.stem: Throughout Matthew 1-2, Joseph is chiefly marked by his:
options: Prompt obedience to God's word in dreams
mc.why: Joseph simply obeys each time God speaks, asking no questions.

mc.stem: Because Matthew repeatedly shows events happening 'that it might be fulfilled,' the unit calls Matthew the Gospel of:
mc.why: Fulfillment is Matthew's recurring note from first verse to last.

mc.stem: The central truth about Jesus' identity in Unit 1 is that He is:
options: The promised King and God with us
mc.why: Unit 1 establishes Jesus as the promised King and Immanuel, God with us.

sa.prompt: Why does Matthew open his Gospel with a genealogy, and what do the titles 'Son of David' and 'Son of Abraham' signify?
sa.model: Matthew opens with a genealogy to lay a foundation for who Jesus is, showing that His coming is no accident but the goal toward which God has worked for two thousand years. The first verse tells us its purpose by calling Jesus the Son of David and the Son of Abraham. Son of David means Jesus is the rightful King, the heir of David's throne whose kingdom the prophets promised would have no end. Son of Abraham means He is the one in whom, as God promised Abraham, all the nations of the earth would be blessed, not the Jews only. Matthew even arranges the list in three sets of fourteen to show a deliberate pattern moving on purpose toward Christ, so the genealogy quietly announces that this child fulfills the whole promise.

sa.prompt: Discuss the women named in the genealogy and what their inclusion teaches about grace.
sa.model: Jewish genealogies normally traced only the fathers, so it is striking that Matthew names four women, and not the honored matriarchs but four marked by scandal or by being outsiders. Tamar deceived Judah; Rahab was a Gentile harlot of Jericho; Ruth was a Moabite whose own people had a fraught history with Israel, yet who is praised in her own book as a woman of noble character; and Bathsheba is named in a way that recalls David's great sin. Their inclusion teaches that grace runs through the very bloodline of the King. The Savior who came to save His people from their sins was not ashamed to be born into a line of sinners and strangers. The lesson presses the point home personally: if a person feels his past disqualifies him, the family tree of Jesus shows there is room for the outsider and the failure, and room for him.

sa.prompt: Explain the meaning of the two names given to the child, 'Jesus' and 'Immanuel.'
sa.model: The child is given two names that together reveal who He is. The name Jesus means the LORD saves, and the angel explains it by saying He will save His people from their sins. This tells us in a single word why He came, not merely to teach or to be admired but to save, and to save from the deepest bondage of all, which is sin. The name Immanuel means God with us, and Matthew draws it from Isaiah to make his boldest claim. This child is not only the King in David's line but God come down to dwell with His people. Many will grant that Jesus was a good man or a teacher and stop there, but this name will not let us stop, for it confesses His deity: in this child the Maker of the heavens is with us.

sa.prompt: Explain the double-fulfillment of Isaiah 7:14, both in the day of Ahaz and in Jesus.
sa.model: The sign of Immanuel in Isaiah 7:14 was first given to King Ahaz, who was threatened by an alliance of enemies and tempted to trust Assyria rather than the LORD. Isaiah told him to ask for a sign; Ahaz hypocritically refused, and Isaiah said God would give a sign anyway, a child called Immanuel. The lesson argues there was a real fulfillment in Ahaz's own day, since a sign set seven hundred years in the future would have meant little to him, likely in the birth of a child whose growing-up marked God's deliverance. Yet the words reach past Ahaz to a greater Son, the virgin's child conceived by the Holy Spirit, who alone is the true and full Immanuel. This is the double fulfillment: the prophecy is real in its first setting and finds its deepest completion in Jesus.

sa.prompt: Explain Hosea 11:1 ('Out of Egypt I called My son') and how recapitulation appears in the 40 years and 40 days.
sa.model: Hosea 11:1 says, Out of Egypt I called My son, and in its original setting it looks back to the nation of Israel being brought up out of Egypt in the Exodus. Matthew sees the words fulfilled again when the child Jesus is brought up out of Egypt after the flight from Herod. The same parallel pattern appears in the wilderness: Israel wandered forty years and failed, while Jesus fasted forty days in the desert and resisted the tempter where the nation had fallen. Scholars call this recapitulation, meaning that Jesus, as the true Israel, relives His people's story and gets it right. God often works things in parallel, so that the first event is true in its own day and the second is truer still, with Jesus succeeding exactly where Israel failed.

sa.prompt: Who were the Magi, and what does their visit reveal about who Jesus is?
sa.model: The Magi were wise men who came from the East, following a star and asking where the one born King of the Jews could be found, for they had come to worship Him. The lesson wants us to feel the wonder that the first worshipers to seek out the newborn King were Gentiles, foreigners from a distant land, while Jerusalem the city of God slept. Their visit reveals that Jesus is not the King of the Jews only but the King for all nations, the Son of Abraham in whom the peoples of the earth are blessed. Already at His birth the nations are being drawn to Him. Their seeking and their worship show that the gospel reaches beyond Israel, and that the proper response to this King, even from outsiders, is to come and bow before Him.

sa.prompt: Contrast Herod and Jesus as two kings set side by side in Matthew 2.
sa.model: Matthew deliberately sets two kings side by side, and the contrast could not be sharper. Herod is troubled when he hears of a newborn King and, to guard his own throne and power, plots murder; outwitted by the Magi, he flies into a rage and orders the slaughter of the baby boys of Bethlehem. Jesus is the true King, born not to seize a throne by violence but to save His people from their sins. One king takes life to protect himself; the other gives His life to rescue others. Herod's fear shows a heart that loves its own power, while the child shows a kingdom built on grace. The lesson notes that from the very beginning the coming of the King is met by the violence of a world that loves its own power, yet it is the gentle King, not Herod, whose reign has no end.

sa.prompt: Describe the three gifts of the Magi and the significance the lesson gives to each.
sa.model: The Magi brought three gifts, and the lesson says each preaches its own small sermon about who the child is. The gold is the tribute fit for a king, pointing to Jesus as the rightful King in David's line. The frankincense is the incense of worship offered to God, pointing to His deity, for Immanuel is God with us. The myrrh is a spice used to anoint the dead, and so even at the cradle it casts a shadow of the cross to come and the death by which He would save His people. Taken together the three gifts confess that this child is King, God, and the one who will die, and that the right response to Him, shown by these Gentile worshipers, is to bow and offer Him our best.

sa.prompt: How does the fulfillment motif tie Matthew 1-2 together into one message?
sa.model: The fulfillment motif is the thread that ties the opening chapters together, because Matthew keeps showing that things happened that it might be fulfilled. The genealogy shows Jesus fulfilling the promises made to David and to Abraham, so that He comes as the long-awaited Messiah and King. The virgin birth fulfills Isaiah's word about Immanuel. The flight to Egypt fulfills Hosea, Out of Egypt I called My Son. The grief at Bethlehem echoes Jeremiah, and even the settling in Nazareth fulfills what the prophets foreshadowed. By repeating this pattern Matthew presents his whole Gospel as the planned completion of Scripture, not an accident of history. The single message is that the King promised in the Law and the Prophets has truly come, and the Old Testament story finds its goal in Jesus.

sa.prompt: What is the central truth about Jesus' identity that Unit 1 establishes before His ministry begins?
sa.model: Before a word of His preaching or a single miracle, Unit 1 establishes the identity of Jesus, which is the foundation for everything else in the Gospel. He is the Son of David, the rightful King and promised Messiah. He is the Son of Abraham, in whom all nations are blessed. He is Jesus, who will save His people from their sins. He is Immanuel, God with us, a name that confesses His deity, for in this child the Maker of the heavens has entered His own creation. He is also the true Israel, fulfilling in Himself the whole story of His people. The central truth is therefore twofold and inseparable: Jesus is the promised King, and He is God with us. Everything Matthew will go on to record about His words and works rests on this answer to the question of who He is.
